<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:right-on-q" data-paper-title="Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-68065f2c5d2ee242">Can OnQ renormalize only the union of teacher and student top-20?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aright-on-q">Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Michigan, Ann Arbor</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Keep a remainder bucket with student residual gradients and teacher smoothing. Truncation would erase tail differences. OPD updates latent weights and scales, with fixed zero point.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If the union covers 90%, the remaining 10% stays a class.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29378v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.29378-right-on-q/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-68065f2c5d2ee242">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:roleq" data-paper-title="RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-roleq-9df6d043" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7153f53110d125bc">Why assign scales by role instead of one stored axis?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aroleq">RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Harvard University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reading and writing map different functional units to rows or columns. Scale those units independently rather than combining writer contributions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>MLP input outputs and MLP output inputs represent corresponding hidden channels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21808">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.21808-roleq/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7153f53110d125bc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:roleq" data-paper-title="RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-cf8caf43e45c624a">Why scale reader outputs but writer inputs in RoleQ?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aroleq">RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Harvard University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reader output units extract information; writer inputs contribute into residual space. A uniform row axis would mix functional units. Exact unweighted ternary vector solutions are not global model optima; full flow includes rotation, compensation, and distillation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One output-projection column spreads one input feature across residual dimensions and needs its own functional scale.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21808">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.21808-roleq/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cf8caf43e45c624a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:roleq" data-paper-title="RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-673a1b11a2492b07">How does exact ternary vector search differ from a fixed threshold?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aroleq">RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Harvard University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Search every nonempty absolute-magnitude sorted prefix for optimal support and scale under the unweighted vector objective. A threshold tries one support; local exactness is not global model optimality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A 0.7×mean threshold can miss a support included in full prefix search.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 结果与独立对照. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21808">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.21808-roleq/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-673a1b11a2492b07">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:roleq" data-paper-title="RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-37dc423488b4064f">Why pack and unpack ternary values and count scales?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aroleq">RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Harvard University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Theoretical trit width is not storage. Pack five trits per byte and count scales and padding; all-zero vectors use zero scale/codes. Nonzero count alone is not byte evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Count tail padding and per-unit scales for 77 weights instead of multiplying by log₂3.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 结果与独立对照. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21808">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.21808-roleq/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-37dc423488b4064f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rope-relay" data-paper-title="Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-rope-relay-6493fdc7" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-bbbbfb21d08ee885">What does RoPERelay fix after selecting sparse KV?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arope-relay">Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Defense Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Retained keys still carry old position phases. Sort temporally, compact coordinates, and align subsequent question and generation without reselecting contents.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Retained positions 0, 100, and 500 require new coordinates and a defined question start.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21126">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.21126-rope-relay/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bbbbfb21d08ee885">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rope-relay" data-paper-title="Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f27fcf57090c69bc">Why rerotate K but not V when compacting sparse KV positions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arope-relay">Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Defense Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Undo each key&#x27;s old rotation then apply its compact position; values reorder without rotation. Align unequal heads to a common right anchor and shift queries/generation. This changes coordinates, not evidence selection; scaled inverse is not simply transpose.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Move old positions ten and 100 to adjacent slots, rerotate K, reorder V, and start questions at the new anchor.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21126">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.21126-rope-relay/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f27fcf57090c69bc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rope-relay" data-paper-title="Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-45411844548681f1">How does position reconstruction differ from prefilling selected text again?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arope-relay">Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Defense Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Invert and reapply key rotations, and reorder V, without recomputing backbone representations. Re-prefill recalculates KV from text and pays a different cost.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Transform existing K rather than concatenating three text spans and processing from layer one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21126">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.21126-rope-relay/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-45411844548681f1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rope-relay" data-paper-title="Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-18d9a4d630ca46ca">Why use a common M rather than per-head continuation positions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arope-relay">Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Defense Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>M is the maximum kept length across layers/heads. Right-align all heads, start questions at M and answer input at M+Q. Different anchors would disagree. Invert scaled RoPE correctly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Heads with eight and four entries both start questions at eight; right-align the four retained entries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21126">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.21126-rope-relay/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-18d9a4d630ca46ca">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:splash" data-paper-title="SPLASH: Switching Parallel Layouts of Attention with Seamless Handoff for LLM Serving" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-splash-7002fc08" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-3e900eeae9381c2c">Why model attention weights and KV ownership together?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asplash">SPLASH: Switching Parallel Layouts of Attention with Seamless Handoff for LLM Serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>TP/DP/CP/DOP assign weights, requests, and caches differently as batches and sequence lengths vary. One ownership model compares memory, communication, and switching.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Four devices have different per-device memory if each request&#x27;s KV is owned or sharded.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37626">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.37626-splash/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3e900eeae9381c2c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:splash" data-paper-title="SPLASH: Switching Parallel Layouts of Attention with Seamless Handoff for LLM Serving" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-6e69fab0b2bf646b">Why amortize SPLASH transitions over remaining generation steps?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asplash">SPLASH: Switching Parallel Layouts of Attention with Seamless Handoff for LLM Serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Layouts distribute attention weights and KV ownership differently, so switching incurs transfer/handoff. Remaining savings must repay that cost under memory limits. Local work is a planner, not CUDA handoff or serving evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Switching can be slower with a few tokens left and useful on a long request.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37626">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.37626-splash/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6e69fab0b2bf646b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:splash" data-paper-title="SPLASH: Switching Parallel Layouts of Attention with Seamless Handoff for LLM Serving" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b271031d58e21d00">How do DOP and TP differ in simplified KV memory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asplash">SPLASH: Switching Parallel Layouts of Attention with Seamless Handoff for LLM Serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>TP uses W_A/T+Bks; DOP uses W_A/T+Bks/T. Both shard weights but distribute KV differently. These are capacity estimates, not measured throughput.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A dominant KV term makes distribution differences more visible.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37626">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.37626-splash/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b271031d58e21d00">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:splash" data-paper-title="SPLASH: Switching Parallel Layouts of Attention with Seamless Handoff for LLM Serving" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-2ca02d5f9707c3f6">How distinguish a transition-aware plan from executing a switch?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asplash">SPLASH: Switching Parallel Layouts of Attention with Seamless Handoff for LLM Serving</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The planner models memory and switch cost. The system must move weights/KV and preserve request state. No local CUDA handoff or B200/H200 performance evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Printing “switch to DOP” does not move cache ownership.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37626">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.37626-splash/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2ca02d5f9707c3f6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:stepquant" data-paper-title="STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-stepquant-3ce3e159" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-cd98bc9cbbbe9a31">Why quantize fixed-size recurrent state instead of only growing KV?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Astepquant">STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each request holds state and repeatedly updates it; concurrency makes fixed state costly and errors can persist. Consider lifetime and spatial block influence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Small state across many requests consumes memory, and early errors can alter later outputs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38169">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.38169-stepquant/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cd98bc9cbbbe9a31">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:stepquant" data-paper-title="STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fdaae29f29c743af">Why allocate STEPQuant bits by remaining state lifetime and key-row impact?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Astepquant">STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Recurrence propagates errors through time, and directions affect readout differently. Allocate block precision under average bits and fit row/column scales. Local budget/error diagnostics are not throughput or renamed uniform INT8.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A small direction that survives many steps may deserve more precision than a large one that soon vanishes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38169">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.38169-stepquant/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fdaae29f29c743af">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:stepquant" data-paper-title="STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7824bc993aefd296">How does spatiotemporal allocation differ from uniform INT8?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Astepquant">STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Allocate more bits to high-risk blocks within a fixed average and use key-row/value-column scaling. Uniform INT8 ignores lifetime and position.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A long-lived, high-impact block can get more bits than a quickly forgotten one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38169">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.38169-stepquant/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7824bc993aefd296">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:stepquant" data-paper-title="STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-dd17ed955bdd5449">Why verify actual average bits instead of the fraction of high-precision blocks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Astepquant">STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Width and block size both determine budget. Minimize weighted error at the actual average, and keep key-row/value-column broadcasting distinct.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Average 4-bit and 8-bit blocks by element counts, not block count alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38169">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.38169-stepquant/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dd17ed955bdd5449">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:taskpress" data-paper-title="TaskPress: Query-Agnostic KV Cache Compression via Task-Guided Pruning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-taskpress-8d6c3897" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-edec647efb03c0f0">Does query agnostic mean no task information?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ataskpress">TaskPress: Query-Agnostic KV Cache Compression via Task-Guided Pruning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Use guide-to-context attention but not the actual query. Task conditioning differs from query-specific selection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Know the task is summarization without knowing the exact future question.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03276v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2608.03276-taskpress/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-edec647efb03c0f0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:taskpress" data-paper-title="TaskPress: Query-Agnostic KV Cache Compression via Task-Guided Pruning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-e794d7481f5d8483">Why use task-guide attention if TaskPress is query agnostic?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ataskpress">TaskPress: Query-Agnostic KV Cache Compression via Task-Guided Pruning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Guide attention supplies reusable task-level preference, combined with value scale, without the actual downstream query. Discard guide KV and retain historical positions. A small kernel does not validate guide generation or multitask gains; full run is not reproduced due to cost.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Summarization guidance can compress text before a future question; reading that question first changes the task.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03276v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2608.03276-taskpress/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e794d7481f5d8483">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:taskpress" data-paper-title="TaskPress: Query-Agnostic KV Cache Compression via Task-Guided Pruning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-63404cd4ee43e665">Why multiply key importance and value scale?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ataskpress">TaskPress: Query-Agnostic KV Cache Compression via Task-Guided Pruning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Guide attention measures read frequency and value scale captures amplitude relevant to quantization. The product accounts for matching and content; either term alone changes the method.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Equal key importance can produce different scores at different value magnitudes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03276v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2608.03276-taskpress/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-63404cd4ee43e665">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:taskpress" data-paper-title="TaskPress: Query-Agnostic KV Cache Compression via Task-Guided Pruning" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-78c797341146a290">Can edge average pooling divide by valid neighbors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ataskpress">TaskPress: Query-Agnostic KV Cache Compression via Task-Guided Pruning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Use odd K, zero padding, and fixed divisor K. Keep original position IDs after gathering, discard guide KV, and note low-index tie-breaking is local.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>At the first token with K=3, still divide by three even if only two neighbors are valid.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03276v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2608.03276-taskpress/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-78c797341146a290">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:twinkv" data-paper-title="TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-twinkv-b8f534bd" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d1d65d81060d202f">Why repair retention under a fixed budget?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atwinkv">TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A base policy can keep redundant keys and drop unique ones. Donor–orphan swaps address gaps without adding entries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Trade one near duplicate for unique older evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27128">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.27128-twinkv/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d1d65d81060d202f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:twinkv" data-paper-title="TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-3a498fa6937cd63c">Why swap redundant donors for orphans rather than raise TwinKV budget?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atwinkv">TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The base eviction can keep duplicates and lose unique evidence. Recover dropped keys without similar retained substitutes by removing redundant retained keys with distant twins. Protect sink/recent items. Key similarity is not semantic equivalence, and reconstruction is not generation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Replace one of two repeated explanations with a unique date at the same cache size.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27128">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.27128-twinkv/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3a498fa6937cd63c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:twinkv" data-paper-title="TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-eccc5ae1290fa1c0">How does TwinKV compose with StreamingLLM or H2O?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atwinkv">TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It repairs a wrapped policy&#x27;s result rather than replacing its score. Compare the same initial policy and KV budget with repair on or off.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>StreamingLLM and StreamingLLM+TwinKV retain equal counts, isolating swaps.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27128">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.27128-twinkv/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-eccc5ae1290fa1c0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:twinkv" data-paper-title="TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-42e6987ceebe0802">Why exclude local twins and sink/recent protected entries from donors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Atwinkv">TwinKV: A Composable Repair Pass for KV Cache Eviction via Pairwise Key Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Find similar retained twins outside the local window and never sacrifice protected entries. Swap only min(orphans, donors) and preserve |R′|=|R|.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Nearby similar keys do not automatically qualify as distant redundancy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27128">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.27128-twinkv/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-42e6987ceebe0802">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:vfold" data-paper-title="VFold: Symmetry-Aware Cross-Layer Value Cache Compression" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-vfold-b54fea4f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4cb9c502c5690b78">What is shared between key and value caches in VFold?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Avfold">VFold: Symmetry-Aware Cross-Layer Value Cache Compression</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Johns Hopkins University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Keys match historical positions; values supply content. Only aligned adjacent-layer values are merged; keys and protected first/last tokens remain separate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two layers can share processed content while retaining independent keys.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12338">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.12338-vfold/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4cb9c502c5690b78">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:vfold" data-paper-title="VFold: Symmetry-Aware Cross-Layer Value Cache Compression" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-5e1e272ca0060eaa">Why align adjacent Value coordinates before sharing, and why use full V for the current token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Avfold">VFold: Symmetry-Aware Cross-Layer Value Cache Compression</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Johns Hopkins University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>CCA and head matching align spaces and fold transforms into V/output weights. Compute full attention for the current token before cross-layer sharing, while keys and protected ends remain independent. Invertible alignment does not make subsequent averaging lossless.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Direct averaging can cancel equivalent features in different coordinates; aligned averaging is still approximate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12338">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.12338-vfold/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5e1e272ca0060eaa">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:vfold" data-paper-title="VFold: Symmetry-Aware Cross-Layer Value Cache Compression" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-38bf50d5f36558a5">How would sharing keys as well as values change VFold?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Avfold">VFold: Symmetry-Aware Cross-Layer Value Cache Compression</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Johns Hopkins University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It would change position matching, not just retrieved content. The documented method keeps keys separate and shares aligned values only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Layer weights over positions can differ even when some values are shared.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12338">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.12338-vfold/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-38bf50d5f36558a5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:vfold" data-paper-title="VFold: Symmetry-Aware Cross-Layer Value Cache Compression" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b09ec1e40fd85a6f">Why fold inverse transforms into every relevant GQA query output slice?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Avfold">VFold: Symmetry-Aware Cross-Layer Value Cache Compression</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Johns Hopkins University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Several query heads share each physical KV head. Apply inverse transforms across all matching output slices. Current token uses full V first, and protected ends add overhead for short sequences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Correcting only one of two query groups leaves the other in mismatched coordinates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与结果. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12338">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.12338-vfold/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b09ec1e40fd85a6f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rescom" data-paper-title="ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-rescom-f00947a9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8dfbcbd312870357">How can a quantized model recover information from the current activation&#x27;s rounding residual?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arescom">ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Quantization maps a range of continuous inputs to one grid value. The forward pass can access both pre-rounding and rounded activations, so their difference retains information the quantized value lost. ResCom reads that residual through a fixed low-rank branch rather than retraining the quantizer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: 1.01 and 1.04 both round to 1.0. Residuals of 0.01 and 0.04 let compensation differ. This is not a model accuracy result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35955v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.35955-rescom/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8dfbcbd312870357">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rescom" data-paper-title="ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f90806934ea200c7">Why does ResCom decompose whitened output cross-statistics rather than truncate the original weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arescom">ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rank should go to residual directions that occur on calibration data and affect outputs. The Gram matrix measures residual scale and correlations; error–residual cross-statistics measure output impact. Cholesky whitening then truncated SVD solves a ridge-regularized output-reconstruction objective. Direct weight truncation ignores residual distribution and solves a different problem.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A large residual may have little output effect while a small one is amplified. Allocate rank by output error, not residual size alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35955v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.35955-rescom/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f90806934ea200c7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rescom" data-paper-title="ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ec528a42e7e51e74">What changes when a low-rank branch sees rounding residuals rather than quantized input?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arescom">ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A branch reading quantized input cannot distinguish two inputs on the same grid point. A residual branch reads the discarded component. ResCom leaves the original path frozen, unlike approaches that remove high-precision weights before quantizing the remainder.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Removing weights before quantization changes calibration; adding UVd+b beside a frozen path does not change its quantization settings.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35955v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.35955-rescom/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ec528a42e7e51e74">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:rescom" data-paper-title="ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-823e70895c07a37a">Why not attach each layer&#x27;s compensation as soon as its statistics are collected?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Arescom">ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Early compensation changes the activations at later layers, so statistics no longer describe the same frozen model. Collect every target layer first, then install branches. Streaming merges only data from the same frozen mapping. G and C are sums: averaging without adjusting ridge changes the solution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Doubling samples doubles G and C, changing a fixed ridge&#x27;s relative strength. Dividing them by sample count is a different objective unless ridge is adjusted.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35955v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.35955-rescom/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-823e70895c07a37a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hope-hilbert" data-paper-title="Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-hope-hilbert-ad1735c1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-678a615e93864162">Why doesn&#x27;t HOPE simply remove neurons with small weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahope-hilbert">Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Scaling a ReLU neuron&#x27;s input and BN scale up and its output weights down can leave the function unchanged. Raw weight magnitude is therefore unreliable. HOPE compares Hilbert-operator capacity from activation functions and output vectors under a Gaussian surrogate, not proven importance on real data.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Multiply the hidden activation by seven and divide output weights by seven. Predictions and functional capacity stay unchanged, although weight magnitude falls.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21366v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2607.21366-hope-hilbert/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-678a615e93864162">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hope-hilbert" data-paper-title="Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-868a387e39220c9a">Why is an input function times an output vector a rank-one operator?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahope-hilbert">Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A neuron returns a scalar activation, which only changes the magnitude along one output-weight vector. The input function maps into one output direction, forming a rank-one tensor. Neuron inner products multiply an activation kernel by the output-vector inner product, not input-weight cosine alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Activation 0.2→0.8 changes 0.2w→0.8w, still along w. Changing the output vector changes functional similarity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 原论文关键图. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21366v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2607.21366-hope-hilbert/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-868a387e39220c9a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hope-hilbert" data-paper-title="Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-16be87c74267c415">Is HOPE Hilbert compression the same as the Hope network in Sleep?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahope-hilbert">Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding analyzes frozen-network functional capacity and compresses with PRUNE, MERGE and EVICT. Sleep&#x27;s Hope is a multi-frequency memory network updated in learning and offline consolidation. Local coverage is the former&#x27;s kernel, pruning and one-step restoration components.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Scoring a frozen ResNet&#x27;s neurons for removal is not teaching a language model during sleep.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 保留机制与接口, 高成本完整实验与复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21366v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2607.21366-hope-hilbert/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-16be87c74267c415">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hope-hilbert" data-paper-title="Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-aa4684949b6038fc">Why freeze initial parameter savings and adjust downstream BN mean during pruning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahope-hilbert">Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The pruning priority divides distortion by initial parameter savings; recomputing from shrinking neighbor shapes changes the criterion. Remove the deleted activation&#x27;s mean contribution from dense consumers&#x27; BN running means to avoid an extra shift. This does not preserve every prediction, and exact undo does not prove lossless accuracy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Mean activation 0.8 and output weights [1,2] imply subtracting [0.8,1.6] from the consumer&#x27;s BN mean, not adding it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议、结果与负控, 高成本完整实验与复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21366v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2607.21366-hope-hilbert/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aa4684949b6038fc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:fold-bias" data-paper-title="Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-fold-bias-1b8893e9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e4fe32856525b65d">Why can&#x27;t a static bias folded into a key be exact for every future query?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afold-bias">Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Independent Researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A key shift contributes a linear function of query, whereas nonzero bias is query-independent. FoldBias fits a direction u so q·u is near 1 on context queries; future drift can increase error. It is distribution-dependent, not an identity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A zero query produces zero logit change from any key shift, not bias 0.8. A query satisfying q·u=1 can express that bias exactly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36520v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36520-fold-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e4fe32856525b65d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:fold-bias" data-paper-title="Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4c1c6936de7640a0">Why rescale a ridge direction to μᵀu=1 rather than use unconstrained least squares?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afold-bias">Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Independent Researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Unconstrained LS trades mean offset against projection spread and may shrink all biases. The paper rescales a ridge-stabilized inverse covariance direction to force mean projection one and minimize spread under that constraint. Covariance divides by N and ridge uses its trace; replacing N with N−1 changes the objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: With one-dimensional μ=2, variance 1 and no ridge, unconstrained LS gives 2/5 and mean projection 0.8. The constrained direction 1/2 gives exactly 1.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36520v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36520-fold-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4c1c6936de7640a0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:fold-bias" data-paper-title="Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-20b2acd190796a3b">Why is FoldBias more informed than deleting bias, but not better for every query?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afold-bias">Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Independent Researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Deletion multiplies bias by zero; folding multiplies by q·u and can be closer to one if future queries resemble calibration. Drift can be worse. The bound also needs bias range and value diameter and compares unrounded keys at fixed values, not a refitted serving stack.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: q·u=0.9 leaves 10% bias error; q·u=−2 gives coefficient 3 vs deletion&#x27;s 1. This is not LLM accuracy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式, 论文离线与线上效果. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36520v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36520-fold-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-20b2acd190796a3b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:fold-bias" data-paper-title="Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-09d707e834f73aa9">Why actually cast keys to BF16 before refitting values?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afold-bias">Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Independent Researcher</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Least squares must see attention from the rounded keys. Fitting with high-precision keys then rounding changes the matrix and invalidates the intended normal equations. The local path casts before building A and returns fit-precision coefficients; cache installation, value rounding and backend correctness need separate validation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: BF16 maps 1.003 to 1.0. Fitting attention with 1.003 compensates an attention table that deployment will not see.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36520v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36520-fold-bias/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-09d707e834f73aa9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:multi-layer-indexer" data-paper-title="Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-multi-layer-indexer-a806ea48" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c9a4d310dd98f418">Why can Multi-layer Indexer overlap indexing and attention when ordinary DSA is sequential?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amulti-layer-indexer">Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · Writer AI Research, Writer Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Ordinary DSA attention waits for its own layer&#x27;s selection. MLI instead consumes an available earlier full-layer selection, allowing the current indexer to work for a later consumer. It changes dependencies and consumption layers rather than making indexing arithmetic disappear.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: While layer two attends layer one&#x27;s selection, its indexer can produce the selection for layer three. Merely launching another stream cannot remove a dependency if attention still waits for its own selection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03768">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.03768-multi-layer-indexer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c9a4d310dd98f418">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:multi-layer-indexer" data-paper-title="Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
