<h2 id="qa-cbe5f04d12d15ba5">Why are retention and lag depth separate parameters?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amulti-layer-indexer">Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · Writer AI Research, Writer Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Retention decides which layers retain indexers. Lag counts predecessor full layers within that retained set. Initial full layers lacking predecessors still follow the standard schedule. Counting physical layers instead of full layers selects the wrong support under sparse retention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: If full layers are 0, 4 and 8, lag one makes layer eight consume layer four&#x27;s selection, not layer seven&#x27;s. Layer zero has no predecessor and must compute its own selection before consuming it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03768">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.03768-multi-layer-indexer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cbe5f04d12d15ba5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:multi-layer-indexer" data-paper-title="Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c32c1710261893ed">Does combining MLI with IndexCache reuse the previous generated token&#x27;s index?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amulti-layer-indexer">Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · Writer AI Research, Writer Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Reuse is across layers of the same current token. Retained full indexers still produce fresh current-token selections. Reusing a previous token adds temporal staleness and is not the reviewed cross-layer schedule.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: At generated token 100, layer four&#x27;s new selection for layer eight still comes from token 100&#x27;s hidden state. Substituting token 99&#x27;s cache changes the algorithm.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03768">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.03768-multi-layer-indexer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c32c1710261893ed">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:multi-layer-indexer" data-paper-title="Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-16f709b859c1316a">Why do a dependency diagram and constant timing on A100 not establish production MLI throughput?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amulti-layer-indexer">Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · Writer AI Research, Writer Inc.</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Execution must join events at first consumption and retain input/output references against allocator reuse. It also needs real SGLang buffers, CUDA graphs and models. The original eight-H200 TP8 long-context setup exceeds a single-card budget, so this batch catalogs it without runtime or fabricated metrics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: Releasing hidden-state references while a side stream still reads them can let the main stream reuse that memory even when diagram arrows are correct. Fixed sleeps neither detect this risk nor measure model throughput.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 已核查与未实现, 成本判断与复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03768">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.03768-multi-layer-indexer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-16f709b859c1316a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:pipnn-ii" data-paper-title="Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and k-NN Graph Building" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-pipnn-ii-e5dbbc9f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f1c1756d337068da">Why does PiPNN II fuse quantized scoring with top-K?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Apipnn-ii">Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and k-NN Graph Building</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-06 · University of Maryland, College Park</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Quantization reduces the bytes read for candidate vectors. Fused scoring immediately compares each new score with the current Kth entry, avoiding a full distance matrix. Fusion reduces traffic for intermediate scores; quantization reduces traffic for input vectors.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A leaf has 100 candidates but needs only the best three. A streaming scorer retains three entries instead of storing and sorting all 100 scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 数据协议与代码映射. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05690v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.05690-pipnn-ii/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f1c1756d337068da">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:pipnn-ii" data-paper-title="Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and k-NN Graph Building" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-dc57958e13deb5d5">Why subtract 128 times the sum of the query bytes after converting database bytes to unsigned?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Apipnn-ii">Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and k-NN Graph Building</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-06 · University of Maryland, College Park</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The instruction multiplies a database byte a = original + 128 by a signed query byte b. This introduces an extra 128b per term; the sum is a correction shared by candidates for the same query. With a zero-sum query the bug disappears, so such queries alone are insufficient tests.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One lane in the original figure has biased dot product 883 and query-byte sum 5. The signed dot product is 883 − 128 × 5 = 243, not 883.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 原论文关键图, 核心公式, 结果、负控与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05690v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.05690-pipnn-ii/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dc57958e13deb5d5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:pipnn-ii" data-paper-title="Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and k-NN Graph Building" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ac52feeffbe422a1">Why not select top-K by integer dot product and apply database scales afterwards?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Apipnn-ii">Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and k-NN Graph Building</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-06 · University of Maryland, College Park</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The scale varies by candidate, so applying it can reverse the order. The negative-dot-product path first applies the database and query scales to each candidate, then keeps the smallest K distances. The positive query scale alone is fixed within a query and does not reorder its candidates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Integer dot products 20 and 10 with row scales 0.1 and 1 become similarities 2 and 10. Selecting by integer dot product picks the wrong winner.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 结果、负控与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05690v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.05690-pipnn-ii/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ac52feeffbe422a1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:pipnn-ii" data-paper-title="Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and k-NN Graph Building" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/compression-and-cache">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Inference compression: weights, KV cache, and serving bandwidth</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f3665f8c57c55373">What negative controls should a CPU streaming top-K use, and does passing them reproduce H100 performance?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Apipnn-ii">Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and k-NN Graph Building</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-06 · University of Maryland, College Park</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use direct signed dots and a full sort as independent references. Test nonzero query sums, unequal scales, tie order, and a single-use iterator. These checks verify scores and ordering, not the quantizer, SIMD/TMA kernels, partitioning, or full-graph speed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: With two equal scaled scores, the reference keeps the earlier candidate; attempting to traverse the stream twice should fail the test. Passing this still measures no Hopper kernel.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 数据协议与代码映射, 结果、负控与边界, 高成本完整实验. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05690v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.05690-pipnn-ii/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f3665f8c57c55373">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>

<details class="ar-learning-guide" markdown="1"><summary>Topic guide and reading order</summary>

## Start with this question

When memory or latency is constrained, do weights, historical states, or data movement dominate?

## Takeaway

AWQ uses calibration activations to identify important channels and applies equivalent scaling to reduce low-bit weight error. GQA shares fewer KV heads across query heads, reducing state per position. KV eviction, quantization, and tiered storage change which tokens are retained, bits per state, and where states reside, respectively. FoldBias does not choose token removals. Given retained keys and fixed bias, it encodes the bias as shared-direction shifts, preserves head width, and refits values after actual cache rounding. Compatibility and quality remain separate tests.

## Example

Moving a prompt from 1k to 32k barely changes weight size but increases KV with sequence length and concurrency. W4 may solve loading but not ever-growing caches. Fewer KV heads, state compression, and eviction can help cache cost; check quantization error or lost evidence for the latter two.

## Common pitfall

Smaller low-bit files do not imply proportional latency reductions: unpack kernels, bandwidth, and batch size matter. Check cache recovery and reuse. Reconstruction error, element counts, and CPU operator success cannot replace GPU throughput or long-context capability measurements.

## Reading order

Read AWQ to see what activation-aware scaling protects, then GQA to understand query-to-KV-head sharing. After separating static weights from dynamic caches, compare eviction, cache quantization, and remote storage.

1. [AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration](../../../../reproductions/2306.00978-awq/README-en.md) · [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978)
2. [GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints](../../../../reproductions/2305.13245-gqa/README-en.md) · [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245)

## Check your understanding

Are AWQ and KV eviction both ways to discard unimportant historical tokens?

??? note "Show suggested answer"

    No. AWQ changes how static weights are represented. KV eviction removes cache positions during inference. The first affects parameter storage and numeric error; the second changes accessible history. Validate quality and resource effects separately.

</details>
